title: Journey to the West
subtitle: Eighty-One Tribulations · A Hundred and Eight Thousand Li of Cloud and Moon
description: Journey to the West is a romantic fantasy novel by the Ming-dynasty writer Wu Cheng'en, and one of the Four Great Classical Novels of Chinese literature. Built on the historical framework of the Tang monk Xuanzang's journey to the Western Heaven for Buddhist scriptures, its flesh and blood come from the mythic imagination of Sun Wukong, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing accompanying their master westward. The result is a magnificent allegory rich in wondrous invention and life's wisdom. Eighty-one tribulations — each one an interrogation of human weakness, each one a step toward enlightenment.

route.title: Journey to the West: Westward Bound — The Scripture-Quest of Subduing Demons and Monsters
route.intro:
You carry the load, I lead the horse — greeting the sunrise, bidding farewell to the sunset. Level the rough road into a thoroughfare, overcome each peril and set out once more.
Wu Cheng'en (c. 1500–1582), style name Ruzhong, literary name Hermit of Sheyang, was a native of Shanyang County in Huai'an Prefecture (modern Huai'an, Jiangsu). A man of extensive learning yet frustrated in the civil examinations, he closed his door in middle age to write, pouring his lifelong understanding of the world's warmth and coldness, his yearning for a free spirit, into this hundred-chapter masterpiece. The image of Sun Wukong — refusing all restraint, wreaking havoc in Heaven — is the literary projection of the Ming-dynasty urban class's burgeoning consciousness of individuality and liberation. From Chang'an's Giant Wild Goose Pagoda to the Flaming Mountains of the Western Regions, from the foot of the Five Elements Mountain to the Thunderclap Monastery of the Western Heaven — let us follow the footsteps of the Tang monk and his disciples along this mythic road that spans east and west, exploring the fantastical world where real national heritage sites and literary imagination intertwine.

stops.title: Stop One: Setting Out from Chang'an · The Journey Begins at the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda
stops.content: In the thirteenth year of Zhenguan (639 AD), the Dharma Master Xuanzang departed from Chang'an to begin his westward journey for scriptures. But the true history is even more magnificent than the novel. In the third year of Zhenguan (629 AD), at the age of twenty-six, Xuanzang risked the death penalty for crossing the border illegally, traveling alone through eight hundred li of shifting sands. In seventeen years and fifty thousand li of travel, he brought back six hundred and fifty-seven volumes of Buddhist scriptures in Sanskrit. The towering Giant Wild Goose Pagoda in Chang'an was built under Xuanzang's direction to preserve the sutras and Buddhist images he brought back from India. Seven stories tall, standing within the Great Mercy Temple, it has been Xi'an's most recognizable landmark for over thirteen hundred years. Climb to the top and gaze down upon the ancient capital of Chang'an — this is where Xuanzang took his first step into the vast Gobi and the unknown. The story of Journey to the West begins here, and the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda is the unfading cover of this epic. The Great Mercy Temple, which houses the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda, was built by Tang Gaozong in memory of his mother, Empress Wende. Xuanzang was appointed its first abbot after his return from India. Here he translated Buddhist sutras for seven years, producing seventy-five texts in one thousand three hundred and thirty-five volumes — an astonishing output, averaging a volume every three days. In the third year of Yonghui (652 AD), to preserve these precious texts and images, Xuanzang personally designed and supervised the construction of the pagoda. It is a square, brick-built, tapered structure modeled after the Indian stupa — it is said that there was a monastery in India where monks saw a flock of wild geese fly past; one broke its wing and fell dead. The monks believed the goose was a Bodhisattva sacrificing its body, and built a pagoda in its memory, calling it the "Goose Pagoda." Xuanzang brought this story back to Chang'an, along with the Buddhist spirit of sacrifice and devotion. In the stone niches flanking the south gate of the pagoda are the "Preface to the Sacred Teachings of the Tripitaka of the Great Tang" by Tang Taizong, Li Shimin, and the "Record of the Preface" by Tang Gaozong, Li Zhi — two emperors composing prefaces and inscriptions for a single monk, an event without parallel in Chinese history. Standing before the pagoda, the grey bricks and mortar seams exude the patina of time. The copper bells hanging from the eaves ring in the wind — ding-dang — crossing thirteen centuries of time. In Wu Cheng'en's novel, the Tang monk and his three disciples set out from Chang'an, but the real Xuanzang was far more alone — without Sun Wukong's seventy-two transformations, without Zhu Bajie's earthy charm, without Sha Wujing's silent loyalty — only a young monk facing eight hundred li of drifting sand with clenched teeth and a steadfast gaze toward the west. The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda has waited here for thirteen hundred years — waiting for every traveler who sets out to return to where they began.

stops.title: Stop Two: Beneath the Five Elements Mountain · The Great Sage Turns to the True Path
stops.content: One of the most unforgettable scenes in Journey to the West is Sun Wukong being pinned under the Five Elements Mountain by the Tathagata Buddha for five hundred years. Not until the Tang Monk passes by and tears away the golden talisman bearing the six sacred words from the mountain's summit does the stone monkey burst free, bow to him as his master, and set out for the west — "The Great Sage Equal to Heaven who wreaked havoc in Heaven five hundred years ago has finally found a master." From that day on, the Sun Wukong who feared neither heaven nor earth gained restraint, direction, and a bond. Though the Five Elements Mountain is fictional, one place embodies the same image of "awakening" — the Songyue Temple Pagoda. The oldest surviving brick pagoda in China, its twelve-sided, densely-eaved structure has withstood fifteen centuries of wind and rain. The Songshan region of Dengfeng has been the first stop for Buddhism entering the central plains since the Han dynasty. The Songyue Temple Pagoda stands like a stabilizing pillar, witnessing the thousand-year eastward transmission of Buddhism. Gazing up at it from below, you can almost hear the earth-shattering cry from five hundred years ago — "Here comes Old Sun!" The Songyue Temple Pagoda was built in the fourth year of Zhengguang, Northern Wei (523 AD). It stands about forty meters tall with fifteen densely stacked eaves, its plan a regular dodecagon — unique in all of China. Seen from a distance, its outline is soft and graceful, each eave slightly upturned, like a giant lotus bud rising from the mountain. On each of four sides of the first story is an arched entrance, its lintel decorated with a flame-shaped pointed arch — the curve of that arch is like the golden fillet on Sun Wukong's head. A five-hundred-year wait compressed into a single stone geometry — the twelve sides represent the twelve links of dependent origination, the fifteen eaves symbolize the stages of cultivation. If Sun Wukong truly had a "Five Elements Mountain," it should be a pagoda like this one: not a yoke that oppresses, but a staircase that guides upward. In Chapter Seven of Journey to the West, the description of Sun Wukong pinned under the Five Elements Mountain is exquisitely poetic: "The mountain took root and sealed itself, growing with every breath like a living thing." Five hundred years later, this "living" mountain was sealed by a golden talisman bearing six words: "Om Mani Padme Hum" — the six-syllable Great Bright Mantra. The instant the Tang Monk tore away the talisman, the mountain split; Sun Wukong leaped from the rubble, knelt, and called "Master!" — the most important turning point in the entire novel. And on Songshan, where the Songyue Temple Pagoda stands, not far away is the Shaolin Temple — where Bodhidharma faced a wall for nine years to "see the nature and realize the Buddha." Shaolin's "wall" and the Five Elements Mountain's "mountain" are essentially the same: both are bondage, and both are cultivation; both are punishment, and both are fulfillment. The Songyue Temple Pagoda's millennium-old dodecagon silhouette is itself like the golden circlet on the Great Sage's head — it bound the Monkey King's wild nature, and in doing so, bound forth his Buddha-nature.

stops.title: Stop Three: Gao Village and the Flowing Sands River · The Brothers Band Together
stops.content: After taking on Sun Wukong, the Tang Monk recruited Zhu Bajie at Gao Village and Sha Wujing at the Flowing Sands River — one gluttonous, lusty, earthy and endearing; the other taciturn yet utterly loyal. With master, three disciples, and the White Dragon Horse, the scripture-questing fellowship was complete. Though Gao Village and the Flowing Sands River are hard to locate on any map, along the ancient Silk Road westward lies a real coordinate of Xuanzang's journey — the Ancient City of Gaochang. When Xuanzang passed through the kingdom of Gaochang, King Qu Wentao tried desperately to keep him there, even threatening to have him sent back to Tang. Xuanzang fasted to show his determination, and in the end moved the king, who not only let him go but provided ample provisions and attendants. The broken walls of Gaochang still stand under the blazing Turpan sun, the earthen ramparts telling of the rise and fall of this Silk Road kingdom through wind and sand — and telling, too, of one seeker's unshakeable faith. The Ancient City of Gaochang lies about forty kilometers east of Turpan, covering an area of two million square meters — one of the largest ancient city ruins on the Silk Road. It is divided into an outer city, inner city, and palace city, its walls all built of rammed earth, the remaining sections still eleven meters high — the earthen yellow ramparts winding like a giant serpent at the foot of the Flaming Mountains. Within the palace city, the Kaghan's Castle retains tall earthen platforms and pagoda foundations. It was here that Xuanzang and King Qu Wentao swore brotherhood. Qu Wentao said to Xuanzang: "Dharma Master, as you journey west, allow me to perform the duties of a host. Please receive my bow." Xuanzang replied: "A man who seeks the Dharma has his heart set on India — I dare not linger." Two equally determined men: one determined to keep, the other determined to leave. Journey to the West transforms Xuanzang's "brotherly oath" with the Gaochang king into the "master-disciple bond" between the Tang Monk and his three disciples. The thirty horses and twenty-five attendants the Gaochang king gave Xuanzang become the White Dragon Horse and the three disciples. The novel turns human warmth into vibrant myth — Zhu Bajie's marriage at Gao Village is a comic expression of attachment to the human world. Sha Wujing, who wore nine skulls around his neck at the Flowing Sands River — those skulls were, the story goes, the bones of the Tang Monk's nine previous incarnations, each devoured by Sha Wujing as they came to the river. Sha Wujing's "cannibal past" hints at a Buddhist concept: cultivation requires accumulating the experience of countless cycles of reincarnation before one can finally cross the sea of birth and death. Beneath the crumbling temple walls of Gaochang, the wind moans through the earthen crevices — like the sound of Zhu Bajie's snores, like Sha Wujing's sutra chanting, like Xuanzang's unspoken farewell to the king of Gaochang.

stops.title: Stop Four: The Flaming Mountains · Three Borrowings of the Plantain Fan
stops.content: When the Tang Monk and his disciples reached the Flaming Mountains, eight hundred li of blazing fire left the land scorched and barren. Sun Wukong had to borrow the Plantain Fan from Princess Iron Fan three times, battling wits and courage across heaven and earth before finally extinguishing the mountain's flames with the help of heavenly troops. This tale perfectly melds the blazing heat of the Western Regions with mythic imagination — summer surface temperatures in the Turpan Basin can exceed seventy degrees Celsius, and the name "Flaming Mountains" is no exaggeration. In the gorge of the Flaming Mountains, the Bezeklik Thousand Buddha Caves (including the Shengjinkou Grottoes) stand as a brilliant representative of Buddhist art from the Gaochang Uighur period. Eighty-three caves are carved into the cliff face in three tiers, their murals blending Han Chinese, Uighur, Persian, and other artistic styles. Standing at the foot of the Flaming Mountains, looking up at these thousand-year-old caves, waves of heat wash over you — this is the same scorching heat that Xuanzang endured step by step as he crossed the Flaming Mountains and pressed on toward India. The furnace blast of the Flaming Mountains did not melt his resolve to seek the scriptures; it purified his faith to the clarity of pure gold. The Bezeklik Thousand Buddha Caves (including the Shengjinkou Grottoes) were first carved during the Qu-family Gaochang period (6th century) and flourished under the Uighur Gaochang period (9th–13th centuries). They form the largest and most richly painted cave complex in the Turpan Basin. The most magnificent is Cave 20, whose murals depict Jataka stories and portraits of Uighur royal donors — Uighur princesses in tall crowns and embroidered robes, Uighur princes holding lotus flowers with delicate features. Yet many of these murals were cut out in the early twentieth century by the German explorer Albert von Le Coq and taken to the Museum of Asian Art in Berlin. What you see in the caves today are large areas of scraped wall, fragmentary outlines, and empty niches. The vermilion sandstone of the Flaming Mountains blazes like actual fire under the noon sun, with surface temperatures often exceeding seventy degrees Celsius — stepping on the ground barefoot will burn you, and an egg buried in the sand will be cooked in fifteen minutes. Standing on the viewing platform, the hot wind hits your face like the instant you open an oven door; the air shimmers into mirages over the distant ground. You suddenly understand why Journey to the West made this a pass that could only be crossed with the Plantain Fan. Not exaggeration — realism. Princess Iron Fan's Plantain Fan "extinguishes fire with one wave, raises wind with a second, and brings rain with a third" — is this not the desert people's longing for a life-giving downpour? Inside the Bezeklik caves, a fragment of a "Vow" mural survives: a row of donors kneel before the Buddha, palms pressed together, eyes devout. What they prayed for, and what Princess Iron Fan finally gave, was the same thing — the will to live on a scorching land. The Flaming Mountains still burn, but the Buddha's smile remains eternally cool.

stops.title: Stop Five: The Lesser Western Heaven · The Yellow-Brow Demon's Trial
stops.content: In Chapter Sixty-Five of Journey to the West, the Tang Monk and his disciples stray into the Lesser Thunderclap Monastery in the Lesser Western Heaven, deceived by the Yellow-Brow Demon disguised as a false Tathagata. Sun Wukong is trapped in a golden gong and can only escape thanks to the horn of the Dragon King of the Metal Element. This trial warns us: the true scriptures are not to be found in grand temple halls, but in the steadfastness of one's own nature. The true Buddha and the false Buddha, the true sutras and the false sutras — all turn on a single thought. Perched atop Phoenix Mountain in Xi County, Shanxi, the Thousand Buddha Temple (also called Lesser Western Heaven), though unrelated to the novel, lives up to its name. Built in the Ming Chongzhen era by Chan Master Dongming, the Great Buddha Hall is a dazzling array of celestial Buddhas and deities — craftsmen used the technique of suspended sculpture to create within a confined space an overwhelming vision of the Western Pure Land, making this the supreme achievement of Chinese suspended-sculpture art. Step into the hall and look up: a thousand Buddhas float in midair, bodhisattvas ride on clouds, and Sanskrit music seems to surge toward you from every direction. Is it real, or is it illusion? Is it Buddha, or is it demon? This is precisely the eternal question posed by the Journey to the West's Lesser Western Heaven trial. The Thousand Buddha Temple sits on a cliff 1,600 meters above sea level on Phoenix Mountain. The name "Lesser Western Heaven" means "a small-scale Western Pure Land" — and it truly is. The Great Buddha Hall covers only 169 square meters, yet within this tiny space it creates a suffocating Buddhist cosmos. The suspended sculptures rise from floor to coffered ceiling, leaving not a single gap — Shakyamuni sits serenely in the center, surrounded by layers of the Ten Great Disciples, the Twelve Perfect Ones, the Eight Legions of Heavenly Beings, and the Twenty-Four Devas. At the highest level, apsaras with streaming robes swoop down from the ceiling; in the middle, bodhisattvas ride lions, elephants, or lotus thrones; at the bottom, dharma-protecting warriors bulge with muscle and glare with rage. The craftsmanship of these suspended sculptures is breathtaking — the artisans first drove wooden pegs into the walls and beams as armatures, wrapped them with straw rope to create volume, then shaped them with a mixture of clay and hemp fibers, finally applying polychrome paint and gold leaf. The most exquisite effect is the figures' "sense of suspension" — each stands on only a tiny cloud support, yet leans forward at thirty to forty degrees, as if about to fly down from the wall at any moment. Standing in the hall and looking up, the celestial host seems to cascade toward you — you feel what the Tang Monk's disciples felt at the Lesser Western Heaven: which is the real Buddha, and which is the false one? The Thousand Buddha Temple's answer is: all Buddhas are real, because all Buddhas are in your own heart. What the Yellow-Brow Demon's false Tathagata deluded was not Sun Wukong's eyes, but his discriminating mind. The finest touch of the Lesser Western Heaven trial is this: the Yellow-Brow Demon is not killed by Sun Wukong, but reclaimed by Maitreya Buddha — because the mind that clings to true and false, to right and wrong, is the hardest demon of all to subdue.

stops.title: Stop Six: Thunderclap Monastery in the Western Heaven · The Attainment of True Enlightenment
stops.content: After enduring eighty-one tribulations, the Tang Monk and his disciples finally reach the Great Thunderclap Monastery on Vulture Peak in the Western Heaven, pay homage to the Tathagata Buddha, and obtain the true scriptures. Yet the Tathagata says that the sutras cannot be transmitted lightly — Ananda and Kashyapa demand a "gift" from the Tang Monk before delivering the wordless true scriptures. This ironic reversal tells us: even on the path to Buddhahood, human conventions cannot be avoided. In the end, they trade their purple-gold alms bowl for the word-filled true scriptures and ride the auspicious clouds of the Eight Great Vajra Guardians back to the Great Tang. In the real world, the Nalanda Monastery in India that Xuanzang reached no longer exists. But in China there are two treasure-houses of Buddhist art worthy of the name "Thunderclap Monastery" — the Beishan Cliff Sculptures in Chongqing, where nearly ten thousand depictions of Guanyin, heavenly kings, and vajra guardians bring the Buddhist cosmos to life along a crescent-shaped cliff, each image imbued with individual personality and emotion; and the Mount Sumeru Grottoes in Ningxia, where over five hundred statues spanning from the Northern Wei to the Tang look down on the world, with the twenty-meter Maitreya Buddha at the northern edge of the Liupan Mountains surveying all beings. Before these two cave sites, the entire wall of divine figures preaches in silence — the destination of the scripture quest is not Vulture Peak; it is in every firm step of the journey itself. The Beishan Cliff Sculptures in Dazu, Chongqing, were first carved in the first year of Jingfu in the late Tang (892 AD) and continued through the Five Dynasties and the two Song dynasties, spanning nearly three hundred years. The most breathtaking is Cave 136, the "Revolving Sutra Library Cave" or "Mind-Wheel Chariot Cave" — at its center stands a massive stone-carved revolving sutra library, with eight dragon pillars spiraling upward like the double helix of DNA, eight coiling dragons rendered in exquisite detail. Inside the cave, Samantabhadra rides a six-tusked white elephant, holding a ruyi scepter with downcast eyes and a faint smile; Manjushri rides a green lion, holding a sutra scroll, his gaze fixed on the distance. The most moving figure is the "Guanyin with Prayer Beads" — her body curves in a gentle S-shape, her fingers lightly touching the beads, her face carrying an otherworldly half-smile. The locals call her the "Coquettish Guanyin" — because her smile holds a maiden's shyness. Buddha is not a wooden statue. The Buddha has feeling. The Mount Sumeru Grottoes in Guyuan, Ningxia, are of a completely different character — rough-hewn, majestic, carrying the wild spirit of the northwest. The Maitreya Buddha in Cave 5 stands 20.6 meters tall, three meters taller than Vairocana Buddha at Longmen — his face is square, his mouth slightly set, his expression solemn rather than compassionate, more like a northern nomadic king. Standing atop Mount Sumeru, the cold wind from the Liupan Mountains nearly blows you off your feet — looking east from here lies the Guanzhong Plain, the very route Xuanzang took westward. Mount Sumeru, Beishan, Longmen, Yungang — these cave complexes scattered across China are like each footprint of the eighty-one tribulations, converging on the path of faith leading to the "Thunderclap Monastery." The final chapter of Journey to the West is deeply moving: the Tang Monk and his disciples return to Chang'an, and Tang Taizong leads his ministers out of the city to welcome them. As Xuanzang unloads the sutras from his horse — the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda witnessed this scene. Thirteen hundred years have passed; the sutras have long been scattered, but the pagoda still stands, the road still lies ahead, and the courage to set out remains. The Tathagata said to the Tang Monk at Thunderclap Monastery: "Your Eastern Land is Jambudvipa, where heaven is high and earth is thick, the people numerous, but full of greed and killing, lust and deceit." He was not speaking of the Eastern Land — he was speaking of every human heart. Every battle fought by the four travelers on the road was a battle against their own greed, anger, and delusion. The scriptures were brought back, but cultivation never ends — just as the bronze bells of the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda have rung for a thousand years, and still ring on.
